title: About Dengue

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Dengue is a viral disease caused by any of the four related viruses.

sections.heading: Types
sections.text: There are four different but closely-related dengue virus types: dengue-1, dengue-2, dengue-3, and dengue-4.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: The most common dengue symptom is fever with:

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Aches and pains (eye pain, typically behind the eyes, muscle, joint, or bone pain)

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Nausea, vomiting

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Rash

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Any warning sign

sections.heading: When to expect symptoms
sections.text: Symptoms of dengue usually begin within 2 weeks after being bitten by an infected mosquito.

sections.heading: When to expect symptoms
sections.text: Symptoms typically last 2–7 days. Most people will recover after about a week.

sections.heading: Areas with Risk of Dengue
sections.text: Dengue transmission is common in tropical and subtropical areas of the world.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Dengue viruses are mainly spread to people by the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: The best way to prevent dengue is to avoid mosquito bites.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: In the United States, there is a dengue vaccine recommended for use in children 9 through 16 with laboratory confirmation of a previous dengue infection, living in areas where dengue is common.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: There is no specific medicine to treat dengue.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: Rest as much as possible.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: Take acetaminophen to control fever and relieve pain.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: See a healthcare provider if you develop a fever or have symptoms of dengue. Tell him or her about your travel.

sections.heading: Vaccines
sections.text: In the United States, there is a dengue vaccine recommended for use in children 9 through 16 with laboratory confirmation of a previous dengue infection, living in areas where dengue is common.

sections.heading: Vaccines
sections.text: The vaccine is not approved for use in U.S. travelers who are visiting but not living in an area where dengue is common.

sections.heading: Personal stories
sections.text: A mother and her 6-year-old daughter are diagnosed with dengue after experiencing sudden fever, rash, body aches, and headaches. In this video, they share their journey from illness to recovery, dengue warning signs, and ways to prevent mosquito bites and the diseases they spread.
